questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: Who among the following founded the Vedanta College in Calcutta to promote both Indian and Western learning?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Raja Rammohan Roy.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Raja Rammohan Roy** founded the Vedanta College in Calcutta in 1825 to promote a blend of **Indian traditional learning** and modern Western education.
 
• He aimed to integrate the teachings of Vedanta philosophy with **scientific and rational education**.
 
• The college emphasized learning English, science, mathematics, and other contemporary subjects alongside traditional Indian scriptures.
 
• Raja Rammohan Roy is widely regarded as the **father of modern Indian Renaissance** for his progressive social and educational reforms.
 
• His educational initiatives were instrumental in laying the foundation for the spread of **modern education in India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmo Samaj:** Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, which was a reformist movement promoting monotheism, equality, and social reform.
 
• **Educational Reforms:** He also played a significant role in advocating for the **abolishment of the traditional Sanskrit-based education** system and supported modern scientific learning.
 
• **Sati Abolition:** Rammohan Roy was a pioneer in the movement to abolish the practice of Sati and worked with the British government to pass the **Regulation XVII in 1829** banning it.
 
• **Journalism Contributions:** He published newspapers like **Sambad Kaumudi** to advocate for social and political reforms, including freedom of the press.
 
• **Legacy:** Rammohan Roy's contributions to education, social reforms, and religious reformation earned him the title of the **"Father of the Indian Renaissance."**
tags: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India

questions.concept: Advent of Europeans
questions.question: In which year did Bakshi Jagabandhu lead the Paika Rebellion to protest against the British land revenue policy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1817**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Paika Rebellion of 1817 was led by **Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar**, the military chief of the Khurda Kingdom, in Odisha.
 
• It was a significant uprising against the **British East India Company’s land revenue policies**, which caused widespread discontent among the Paikas and other sections of society.
 
• The rebellion began in Khurda and rapidly spread to other regions of Odisha, involving a broad coalition of peasants, zamindars, and tribal groups.
 
• The British imposed exploitative taxes, disrupted traditional land rights, and confiscated the hereditary estates of many zamindars, fueling the revolt.
 
• The Paikas, traditional militia of Odisha, were primarily affected as their role in the Khurda kingdom was marginalized due to British administrative reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Who were the Paikas?**

 
 
• The Paikas were the traditional landed militia of Odisha who rendered military service to the kings of the Khurda Kingdom in exchange for land grants.
 
• Their hereditary land tenures were known as "jagir," which the British abolished, reducing them to poverty.
 
 
 
• **Impact of British Revenue Policies:**
 
 
• The introduction of Permanent Settlement in Bengal and parts of Odisha disrupted the traditional agrarian system.
 
• The British confiscated lands and auctioned them off to new landlords, alienating the Paikas and local zamindars.
 
 
 
• **Key Events of the Rebellion:**
 
 
• The rebellion began in March 1817, with the Paikas attacking British establishments and burning government buildings.
 
• It was suppressed by September 1817, as the British used superior military technology and administrative measures.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Paika Rebellion:**
 
 
• The Paika Rebellion is often regarded as a precursor to India's First War of Independence in 1857.
 
• In 2017, the Government of India commemorated the 200th anniversary of the rebellion, recognizing its historical significance.

questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: Who among the following was known for promoting inter-caste and inter-religious marriages through legislation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Raja Ram Mohan Roy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** was a key social reformer in India during the 19th century.
 
• He strongly advocated for progressive reforms, including the promotion of **inter-caste and inter-religious marriages**.
 
• Roy was instrumental in the abolition of **Sati** and worked towards improving women's rights, aligning with his broader reformist agenda.
 
• He founded the **Brahmo Samaj** in 1828, which championed social and religious reforms and encouraged egalitarian values.
 
• His efforts laid the foundation for modern Indian society by promoting **rationalism, equality, and universal human rights.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Inter-caste and inter-religious marriages:** These marriages are a union between individuals from different castes or religions, challenging traditional norms and promoting social integration.
 
• **Brahmo Samaj:** A socio-religious reform movement founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy. It emphasized monotheism, rational thought, and rejection of caste discrimination.
 
• **Sati:** A historical practice in which a widow was immolated on her husband's funeral pyre. Raja Ram Mohan Roy was pivotal in its abolition through legislation in 1829.
 
• **Social reform in British India:** Reform movements during the colonial period aimed at addressing societal issues such as caste hierarchy, gender inequality, and religious orthodoxy.
 
• **Legacy:** Raja Ram Mohan Roy is regarded as the "Father of Modern India" for his efforts in modernizing Indian society and promoting progressive ideals.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which of the following acts authorised the Governor General to override his council in matters affecting the interest of British empire in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act of 1793**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Charter Act of 1793** was instrumental in reinforcing the power of the Governor-General of India in certain critical matters.
 
• It authorised the Governor-General to **override the decisions of his council** in cases where the interests of the British Empire in India were at stake.
 
• This act was an extension of the **Regulating Act of 1773** and **Pitt’s India Act of 1784**, further centralising power in the hands of the Governor-General.
 
• The provision was seen as a measure to ensure the efficient administration of British interests in India without unnecessary delays caused by council disagreements.
 
• The act also renewed the East India Company’s charter for another 20 years, maintaining its monopoly over trade with India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1813:**

 
 
• This act ended the East India Company’s trade monopoly in India, except for trade in tea and trade with China.
 
• It allowed Christian missionaries to propagate their religion in India.
 
• It allocated funds for the promotion of education in India.
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act of 1773:**
 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British Parliament to regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.
 
• It created the position of the Governor-General of Bengal and established a council to assist him.
 
 
 
• **Pitt's India Act of 1784:**
 
 
• This act established a system of dual control by creating a Board of Control in Britain to supervise the East India Company’s administration in India.
 
• It distinguished between the company’s commercial and political functions.
 
 
 
• **Centralisation of Power:**
 
 
• The Charter Act of 1793 was part of the broader British strategy to centralise administrative power in India for better governance and control.
 
• This trend continued in subsequent acts, culminating in the complete transfer of power to the British Crown under the Government of India Act 1858.
tags: India under East India Company’s Rule

questions.concept: The Great Revolt of 1857
questions.question: Which event marked the final collapse of the British policy of annexation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Revolt of 1857**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Revolt of 1857**, also known as the **First War of Indian Independence**, marked a turning point in the history of British rule in India.
 
• It was a widespread but unsuccessful rebellion against the **British East India Company** rule.
 
• The revolt was triggered due to various factors such as **economic exploitation, political annexation, religious interference, and social injustices**.
 
• One of the key policies that fueled resentment was the **Doctrine of Lapse**, implemented by Lord Dalhousie, which allowed the British to annex Indian princely states if the rulers did not have a direct heir.
 
• The annexation of states like **Awadh** further intensified the discontent among Indian rulers and the local population.
 
• The rebellion was led by figures such as **Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Tantia Tope, Nana Sahib**, and others, who became symbols of resistance.
 
• The revolt demonstrated the widespread dissatisfaction among Indians and revealed the **limitations of the British policies of annexation**.
 
• After suppressing the revolt, the British Crown took direct control of India through the **Government of India Act, 1858**, ending the era of East India Company rule.
 
• The revolt marked the final collapse of the British annexation policy, and subsequent rulers adopted a more cautious approach towards governance and administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Partition of Bengal**__

 __
 
• The **Partition of Bengal** in 1905 by Lord Curzon was a significant event in Indian history. It divided Bengal into **East Bengal and West Bengal** based on religious and administrative reasons.
 
• The move was seen as an attempt to divide Hindus and Muslims and weaken the nationalist movement.
 
• The widespread protests against the partition led to the growth of the **Swadeshi Movement** and ultimately resulted in the reversal of the partition in 1911.
 
 
 
• **Quit India Movement**__
 __
 
• The **Quit India Movement** was launched by the Indian National Congress on **8 August 1942** under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• It demanded an end to British rule in India and was characterized by widespread protests, strikes, and civil disobedience.
 
• Unlike the Revolt of 1857, this movement was non-violent but still faced brutal suppression by the British authorities.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1935**__
 
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1935** was the longest Act passed by the British Parliament concerning India.
 
• It introduced significant reforms, including the establishment of provincial autonomy and the creation of the **Federal Court**.
 
• This Act laid the foundation for the federal structure of governance but did not address the complete independence aspirations of Indians.
tags: The Great Revolt of 1857

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: According to the Regulating Act of 1773 of the East India Company, to whom did the governors of Madras and Bombay report regularly?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The Governor General**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Regulating Act of 1773** was an important legislative measure passed by the **British Parliament** to regulate the affairs of the **East India Company** in India.
 
• The act created the position of the **Governor General of Bengal**, who was given supervisory authority over the governors of **Madras and Bombay.**
 
• The **Governor General** was tasked with overseeing and ensuring better coordination between the presidencies of Madras, Bombay, and Bengal.
 
• This act marked the beginning of a centralized administration in India and aimed to curb the corruption and inefficiency prevalent in the **East India Company's governance.**
 
• The first **Governor General** appointed under the Regulating Act was **Warren Hastings.**
 
• The governors of Madras and Bombay were required to report regularly and act according to the directives of the **Governor General** to ensure uniformity in policies and governance.
 
• The **Regulating Act** also established a **Supreme Court** in Calcutta to handle legal issues, further strengthening the role of the Governor General.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The British Parliament**__

 __
 
• The **British Parliament** passed the Regulating Act of 1773 but did not directly oversee the operations of the **East India Company's presidencies.**
 
• The act aimed to reduce the company's autonomy and introduce a centralized administrative system.
 
• The Parliament had the power to legislate but did not directly manage the day-to-day affairs of the Indian presidencies.
 
 
 
• **Court of Directors**__
 __
 
• The **Court of Directors** was responsible for overseeing the commercial and administrative aspects of the **East India Company.**
 
• They were based in **London** and played a role in policymaking but did not directly supervise the governors of Madras and Bombay.
 
• The Court of Directors reported to the **British Parliament** rather than directly managing presidencies.
 
 
 
• **The British Crown**__
 
 
• The **British Crown** was involved in India's governance later, especially after the **Government of India Act 1858**, which transferred control from the East India Company to the Crown.
 
• During the time of the Regulating Act of 1773, the Crown did not directly manage the presidencies or supervise their governors.
tags: India under East India Company’s Rule

questions.concept: Changes in Indian Administration after 1858
questions.question: The first Law Commission in India was headed by ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Macaulay**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first Law Commission in India was established in 1834 under the Charter Act of 1833.
 
• Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay was appointed as the Chairman of the First Law Commission.
 
• The Commission was tasked with codifying Indian laws and making them uniform across the country.
 
• One of its significant achievements was the drafting of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which was later enacted in 1860.
 
• The work done by the Law Commission under Macaulay laid the foundation for the modernization of the Indian legal system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1833:**

 
 
• This Act was a landmark legislation by the British Parliament that centralized legislative authority in India.
 
• It marked the beginning of law codification in India and led to the formation of the First Law Commission.
 
• The Act also abolished the East India Company's monopoly on trade.
 
 
 
• **Indian Penal Code (IPC):**
 
 
• The IPC was drafted by the First Law Commission under Lord Macaulay's leadership.
 
• It serves as the primary criminal code for India, covering offenses and their punishments.
 
• Enacted in 1860, it has undergone several amendments but remains a cornerstone of Indian criminal law.
 
 
 
• **Law Commission of India:**
 
 
• It is an executive body established by the Government of India to recommend legal reforms.
 
• The Commission was first formed during British rule and continues to function in post-independence India.
 
• It is reconstituted every few years to study specific legal issues and suggest amendments or new laws.
 
 
 
• **Lord Macaulay's Contribution:**
 
 
• Besides legal reforms, Macaulay is known for his role in introducing English education in India.
 
• His famous "Minute on Education" argued for the promotion of English as the medium of instruction.
 
• He played a critical role in shaping the administrative and legal landscape during British rule in India.
tags: Changes in Indian Administration after 1858

questions.concept: The Great Revolt of 1857
questions.question: Who among the following was an old zamindar from Bihar who joined the rebel sepoys during the Revolt of 1857 and battled with the British for many months?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Kunwar Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kunwar Singh** was a prominent leader of the **Indian Revolt of 1857**, also known as the First War of Indian Independence.
 
• He was an **aged zamindar** from the state of **Jagdishpur in Bihar** and belonged to the Rajput community.
 
• Despite being in his **80s**, Kunwar Singh demonstrated remarkable bravery and leadership during the revolt.
 
• He led the rebel sepoys in **Bihar** and fought against British colonial forces for several months.
 
• Kunwar Singh strategically retreated and waged a guerrilla war, which proved to be a significant challenge for the British.
 
• He is remembered for his resilience and his role in uniting the locals against British rule in the region.
 
• His efforts made him one of the most notable figures of the 1857 rebellion, earning him the title of a **freedom fighter**.
 
• Kunwar Singh is commemorated as a symbol of patriotism and resistance against colonial oppression in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bakht Khan**__

 __
 
• **Bakht Khan** was a key leader in the Revolt of 1857 and served as the **Commander-in-Chief of the rebel forces** in Delhi.
 
• He was a **subedar** in the British East India Company’s army before joining the rebellion.
 
• Bakht Khan is known for his leadership in coordinating the rebel forces and establishing an administrative system in Delhi under the nominal leadership of **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
 
 
 
• **Tantia Tope**__
 __
 
• **Tantia Tope** was another significant leader of the Revolt of 1857 and a close associate of **Rani Lakshmibai**.
 
• He is known for his guerrilla warfare tactics, which caused significant challenges for the British forces.
 
• Tantia Tope was instrumental in the rebellion in the region of **Central India**.
 
 
 
• **Ahmadullah Shah**__
 
 
• **Ahmadullah Shah**, also known as the **Maulavi of Faizabad**, was a key leader during the 1857 revolt.
 
• He was a religious leader and played a significant role in mobilizing people against British rule in the **Awadh** region.
 
• He is remembered for his efforts to unite Hindus and Muslims to fight against the colonial powers.

questions.concept: Advent of Europeans
questions.question: In which year did Francois Martin establish Pondicherry, which later emerged as the Headquarters of the French in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1674**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Francois Martin** established Pondicherry in **1674** as a French trading settlement.
 
• Pondicherry became the **Headquarters of French India**, serving as the political and commercial hub for French activities in the region.
 
• Francois Martin was the first **Governor-General of French India**, playing a significant role in expanding French influence in southern India.
 
• The French East India Company chose Pondicherry for its strategic location along the Coromandel Coast, enabling access to regional trade networks.
 
• The settlement marked the beginning of French colonial rule in India, which lasted until the mid-20th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pondicherry's Historical Significance:**

 
 
• Pondicherry, now Puducherry, was a key colonial port and administrative center during French rule.
 
• The city retains its French heritage through architecture, language, and cultural practices.
 
 
 
• **French East India Company:**
 
 
• Established in 1664, the French East India Company aimed to compete with other European trading companies in Asia.
 
• It focused on trade in spices, textiles, and other goods from India and Southeast Asia.
 
 
 
• **Francois Martin's Contributions:**
 
 
• Francois Martin laid the foundation for French colonial expansion in India by fostering trade and alliances with local rulers.
 
• He played a critical role in defending Pondicherry against rival European powers and regional conflicts.
 
 
 
• **French Colonial Legacy in India:**
 
 
• The French retained territories like Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, and Yanam until their integration into India in 1954.
 
• The influence of French culture and governance continues to shape these regions, especially in architecture and cuisine.
tags: Advent of Europeans

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which of the following acts provided a regular code of all regulations that could be enacted for the internal Government of British India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pitt’s India Act 1784**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Pitt’s India Act 1784 was introduced by the British Parliament to address the shortcomings of the Regulating Act of 1773.
 
• It established a system of dual control, dividing powers between the British Crown and the East India Company for the governance of British India.
 
• The Act created a Board of Control in Britain to supervise the administration of India and ensure a regular code for internal governance.
 
• This legislation marked the first significant step toward centralizing British control over Indian administrative matters.
 
• It laid the groundwork for future legislative and administrative reforms in British India, ensuring a more structured approach to governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Regulating Act 1773:**

 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British Parliament to regulate the activities of the East India Company in India.
 
• It established the office of the Governor-General of Bengal and a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
 
• However, it lacked clear provisions for effective control, leading to administrative inefficiencies.
 
 
 
• **Charter Act of 1813:**
 
 
• It ended the trade monopoly of the East India Company, except for trade in tea and trade with China.
 
• It allowed Christian missionaries to propagate their religion in India for the first time.
 
• It earmarked funds for the promotion of education in India.
 
 
 
• **Charter Act of 1793:**
 
 
• This Act renewed the East India Company’s charter for another 20 years.
 
• It granted the company the authority to raise revenue and carry on administrative functions in India.
 
• It reaffirmed the supremacy of the British Crown over the company’s affairs.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Pitt’s India Act:**
 
 
• It introduced significant checks and balances to avoid mismanagement in India.
 
• The Board of Control ensured that the company’s decisions aligned with British interests.
 
• This Act marked the beginning of British Parliament’s direct involvement in Indian governance.
tags: India under East India Company’s Rule

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: The British used education as a tool to ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**strengthen colonial rule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The British introduced modern education in India primarily to create a class of educated Indians who could assist in administrative tasks, thereby strengthening colonial control.
 
• The English Education Act of 1835, spearheaded by Thomas Babington Macaulay, promoted Western knowledge and English as the medium of instruction to serve colonial interests.
 
• Educated Indians were intended to act as intermediaries between the British rulers and the Indian population, ensuring smoother governance.
 
• The curriculum emphasized British history, culture, and values, aiming to instill loyalty to the colonial government and suppress any anti-colonial sentiment.
 
• This education policy created a workforce for clerical and subordinate positions in the British administration, fulfilling the economic and political needs of the Empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Macaulay’s Minute (1835)**

 
 
• Thomas Babington Macaulay advocated for the promotion of English education in India, emphasizing Western literature and science over traditional Indian knowledge systems.
 
• His famous "Minute on Indian Education" argued that educating a small elite group in English would create a class of individuals "Indian in blood and color but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect."
 
 
 
• **Wood’s Despatch (1854)**
 
 
• Known as the "Magna Carta of English Education in India," it laid the foundation for systematic education in the country.
 
• It recommended the establishment of universities in major cities and schools across various levels, with English as the primary medium of instruction for higher education.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Colonial Education**
 
 
• Led to the emergence of a new middle class, which played a significant role in the Indian independence movement.
 
• Undermined traditional Indian education systems and cultural values.
 
• Created social divisions, as access to education was limited to a privileged few.
 
 
 
• **Downward Filtration Theory**
 
 
• It was the idea that educating a small elite group would eventually lead to the spread of knowledge and Western values to the broader population.
 
• This theory justified the limited investment in mass education by the British colonial government.
tags: India under East India Company’s Rule

questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: The Singh Sabha movement is associated with which community?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sikh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Singh Sabha Movement was a reform movement among Sikhs in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, initiated to revive Sikhism's distinct identity and religious practices.
 
• It began in **Amritsar in 1873** and later expanded to Lahore, forming the Lahore Singh Sabha in 1879.
 
• The movement sought to counter the influence of Christianity, Hindu reform movements, and western ideologies on Sikh practices and traditions.
 
• It emphasized the promotion of Sikh education, the Gurmukhi script, and the teachings of Guru Granth Sahib while opposing superstitions and rituals that deviated from core Sikh principles.
 
• The Singh Sabha was instrumental in the establishment of institutions like the **Khalsa College in Amritsar** and in publishing Sikh literature to spread awareness about Sikh history and values.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Objectives of the Movement:**

 
 
• To restore Sikhism to its original form by eliminating practices like idol worship and caste discrimination that had crept into the community.
 
• To assert the unique identity of Sikhs as distinct from Hindus and Muslims.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Education:**
 
 
• The movement led to the establishment of modern educational institutions, such as Khalsa Schools and Colleges, to educate Sikhs in both religious and secular fields.
 
• It played a crucial role in encouraging women’s education within the Sikh community.
 
 
 
• **Role of Key Leaders:**
 
 
• Prominent leaders like **Bhai Gurmukh Singh**, **Baba Khem Singh Bedi**, and **Professor Gurmukh Singh** spearheaded the movement.
 
• They worked on translating Sikh scriptures and historical texts into accessible languages to disseminate Sikh teachings widely.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Singh Sabha Movement:**
 
 
• The movement laid the foundation for the **Gurdwara Reform Movement** in the early 20th century, which ultimately led to the establishment of the **Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC)**.
 
• It remains a pivotal chapter in the history of Sikhism, reinforcing its distinct religious and cultural identity.

questions.concept: Advent of Europeans
questions.question: Which of the following companies assisted the Raja of Cochin in expelling the Portuguese from his kingdom in 1663?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __** Dutch East India Company**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In **1663**, the **Dutch East India Company **(Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie or VOC) assisted the** Raja of Cochin in ousting the Portuguese from his kingdom**.
 
• The Portuguese had established their presence in Cochin since the early 16th century, using it as a key port for trade in spices.
 
• The Dutch aimed to dominate the spice trade in the Malabar Coast and saw the Portuguese as their primary competitors.
 
• The** Dutch captured Cochin and other Portuguese territories in the region**, marking a significant shift in colonial power dynamics in South India.
 
• This event was part of a broader conflict between European colonial powers over control of trade routes and resources in Asia.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Portuguese in India:**

 
 
• The Portuguese were the first European colonial power to establish a stronghold in India, starting with Vasco da Gama's arrival in Calicut in 1498.
 
• Cochin was one of their earliest and most important bases, established in 1503.
 
• They controlled trade in spices like pepper, cardamom, and cinnamon from the Malabar Coast.
 
 
 
• **Dutch East India Company (VOC):**
 
 
• Founded in 1602, the VOC was a powerful trading corporation that sought to monopolize trade in the East Indies (modern-day Indonesia and surrounding areas).
 
• It played a significant role in colonial expansion in Asia, particularly in the spice trade.
 
• The VOC set up trading posts in various parts of India, including Surat, Nagapattinam, and Cochin.
 
 
 
• **Conflict Between European Powers:**
 
 
• The 16th and 17th centuries saw intense rivalry between European powers like the Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British for control of trade in Asia.
 
• These conflicts often involved alliances with local rulers, as seen in the Dutch support for the Raja of Cochin.
 
• Such rivalries eventually led to the decline of Portuguese influence in India and the rise of Dutch and later British dominance.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Cochin:**
 
 
• Cochin (modern-day Kochi, Kerala) was a major port city and trade hub on the Malabar Coast.
 
• It was strategically important for controlling the spice trade, which was highly lucrative in the European markets.
 
• The region's rich resources and trade opportunities attracted multiple colonial powers over centuries.

questions.concept: Socio - Religious Reform Movements in the 19th and 20th CE India
questions.question: One important outcome of British social reforms was ______.

options.text: emergence of women in public life

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**emergence of women in public life**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The British social reforms in India during the 19th and early 20th centuries played a crucial role in addressing key social issues like **sati, child marriage, and widow remarriage**.
 
• These reforms, driven by British administrators and Indian reformers, led to the creation of laws like the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856**, which encouraged gender equality.
 
• Education for women was promoted through initiatives like **introducing girls' schools** and supporting Indian reformers such as **Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**.
 
• Women began participating in public life, taking up professions such as teaching and social work, and eventually contributing to the **freedom movement**.
 
• The active involvement of women in public spheres laid the foundation for their increasing role in politics, education, and social reform in independent India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sati Abolition:**

 
 
• The practice of sati (self-immolation of widows) was abolished through the efforts of reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and legislation such as the **Bengal Sati Regulation Act of 1829**.
 
• The abolition marked a significant step towards improving the status of women in Indian society.
 
 
 
• **Educational Reforms:**
 
 
• British missionaries and Indian reformers worked to establish schools for girls, breaking societal barriers to female education.
 
• Pioneering institutions like the **Bethune College** in 1849 became symbols of progress in women's education.
 
 
 
• **Role of Indian Reformers:**
 
 
• Leaders like Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar championed the cause of widow remarriage and girls' education.
 
• Reformers played a pivotal role in bridging the gap between British policies and Indian social realities.
 
 
 
• **Women in Freedom Movement:**
 
 
• Prominent figures like **Sarojini Naidu, Kasturba Gandhi, and Annie Besant** emerged as key leaders in India's struggle for independence.
 
• Their active participation was a direct result of the social reforms initiated in the preceding decades.
 
 
 
• **Lasting Impact:**
 
 
• The reforms initiated during the British era laid the groundwork for constitutional provisions like **gender equality** in independent India.
 
• Women’s increasing role in education, professions, and politics today can be traced back to these transformative social reforms.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: The Charter Act of 1833 created a separate ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Law Commission in India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Charter Act of 1833 was a significant legislation passed by the British Parliament to reorganize the administration in India.
 
• It centralized the administration by vesting legislative power in the Governor-General of India and his council.
 
• The act led to the establishment of the first **Law Commission in India** in 1834 under the chairmanship of Lord Macaulay.
 
• The Law Commission was tasked with codifying Indian laws, which ultimately resulted in the drafting of the Indian Penal Code (1857).
 
• This act also marked the beginning of the end of the East India Company's commercial activities, focusing solely on governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Acts:**

 
 
• The Charter Acts were a series of legislative measures passed by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company’s operations in India.
 
• The Charter Act of 1813 allowed missionaries to propagate Christianity in India and ended the monopoly of the East India Company except for the tea trade.
 
• The Charter Act of 1853 marked the last in the series and led to the initiation of the Indian Civil Services examination.
 
 
 
• **Indian Penal Code (IPC):**
 
 
• The IPC, drafted by the first Law Commission, was completed in 1837 but enacted in 1860 after revisions.
 
• It remains the primary criminal code in India, though it has undergone amendments over the years.
 
 
 
• **Lord Macaulay:**
 
 
• Thomas Babington Macaulay was a British historian and politician who played a key role in introducing English education and legal reforms in India.
 
• He is best known for his "Minute on Education" (1835) and his role in drafting the Indian Penal Code.
 
 
 
• **Governance Changes under the Charter Act of 1833:**
 
 
• It made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India, centralizing authority.
 
• It introduced provisions to admit Indians into government service, though not effectively implemented.

questions.concept: Advent of Europeans
questions.question: The Dutch East India Company's trade on the Coromandel Coast registered a significant increase over the 17th century due to:

options.text: the establishment of trading posts in Goa and Surat
an increase in the demand for textile from the south-east Asian markets
the decline and collapse of the British influence in the region

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**an increase in the demand for textile from the south-east Asian markets**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Coromandel Coast emerged as a major center for textile production during the 17th century, with its textiles highly sought after in South-East Asian markets.
 
• South-East Asia exhibited a rising demand for Indian textiles such as chintz, calicoes, and muslin due to their quality and intricate designs.
 
• The Dutch East India Company capitalized on this demand by expanding its trade network and establishing robust maritime routes linking India and South-East Asia.
 
• Indian textiles were used in barter trade by the Dutch to acquire spices, particularly from Indonesia, which further boosted commerce on the Coromandel Coast.
 
• The strategic presence of Dutch trading posts along the Coromandel Coast facilitated large-scale exports, cementing the region's importance in global trade during the 17th century.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Coromandel Coast:** Located in southeastern India, it was renowned for its production of high-quality textiles, particularly cotton fabrics.
 
• **Dutch East India Company (VOC):** Established in 1602, the VOC was a major trading enterprise that controlled trade networks between Europe, Asia, and the Indian subcontinent.
 
• **Textiles as Trade Commodities:** Indian textiles were highly valued in South-East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, often exchanged for spices, precious metals, and other goods.
 
• **Spice Trade Connection:** The Dutch used Indian textiles to acquire spices like nutmeg, cloves, and pepper from islands in South-East Asia, creating a mutually beneficial trade system.
 
• **Globalization of Indian Textiles:** The flourishing textile trade during the 17th century contributed significantly to India's integration into the global economy of the early modern period.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which of the following acts of the East India Company mandated that selection for civil employees in British Indian territory would be based on the competitive examinations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act 1853**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Charter Act of 1853** was the last Charter Act passed by the British Parliament concerning the East India Company.
 
• This Act introduced an open and competitive system of recruitment for civil services, marking a significant departure from the patronage system.
 
• The Act mandated that civil service positions in the British Indian administration would be filled through a competitive examination process.
 
• The competitive examinations were to be conducted in England, and the system was open to all British citizens, including Indians, although Indians faced significant barriers initially.
 
• The Act reflected growing demands for administrative reforms and efficiency in the governance of British India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1793:** This Act renewed the East India Company's charter for 20 years but did not introduce any significant administrative reforms.
 
• **Pitt's India Act of 1784:** It established a dual system of governance, creating the Board of Control to supervise the East India Company’s civil, military, and revenue affairs.
 
• **Charter Act of 1813:** This Act ended the East India Company’s trade monopoly in India, except for trade in tea and trade with China.
 
• **Impact of the Charter Act of 1853:** It was the first step toward introducing a merit-based system in Indian civil services, which was later formalized under the Indian Civil Service Act of 1861.
 
• **Significance of Competitive Exams:** The provision for competitive examinations laid the foundation for modern civil services in India and reflected the influence of liberal ideas of equality and meritocracy.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: When were the Municipal Corporations of Calcutta and Bombay established?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1726**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Municipal Corporations of Calcutta (now Kolkata) and Bombay (now Mumbai) were established in the year **1726**.
 
• They were formed under the provisions of the **Charter of 1726**, issued by the British East India Company.
 
• This Charter led to the establishment of a **Mayor's Court** and municipal governance systems in these cities.
 
• The primary objective was to improve urban administration and cater to the needs of a growing British population in these trading hubs.
 
• These were among the earliest attempts at formal municipal governance in India during the colonial period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter of 1726:**

 
 
• It was issued by King George I of Britain at the request of the British East India Company.
 
• The Charter introduced a system of civil and criminal courts in the presidency towns of Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.
 
• This laid the foundation for modern municipal governance in India.
 
 
 
• **Municipal Governance in Colonial India:**
 
 
• The British introduced municipal governance to ensure better administration, sanitation, and urban development in growing cities.
 
• Municipal corporations were primarily established in trading centers like Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Urban Local Bodies:**
 
 
• The Indian Councils Act of 1861 and 1882 further developed local self-governance in India.
 
• In 1882, Lord Ripon, known as the “Father of Local Self-Government in India,” introduced reforms to make municipal bodies more representative.
 
 
 
• **Current Status:**
 
 
• Today, municipal corporations in India operate under the provisions of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992).
 
• This amendment provides constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) for decentralized governance.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: Which of the following was the final court of appeal for India under British rule?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Privy Council in London**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Privy Council in London served as the **highest court of appeal** for India during British rule.
 
• It was established as the final judicial authority to resolve disputes from colonies, including India, under the British Empire.
 
• Indian cases were appealed to the Privy Council after decisions from the Federal Court or provincial courts under colonial judicial hierarchy.
 
• The Privy Council's decisions were binding and considered the ultimate authority in legal matters during British rule.
 
• After independence, the jurisdiction of the Privy Council over Indian cases was abolished with the enactment of the **Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948**, and later replaced by the Supreme Court of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federal Court of India**

 
 
• Established in 1937 under the **Government of India Act, 1935** to function as India's highest court below the Privy Council.
 
• It dealt with disputes between provinces and the central government and had appellate jurisdiction over certain cases.
 
• Its role was significant but limited compared to the Privy Council.
 
 
 
• **Privy Council's Role**
 
 
• The Privy Council was composed of legal experts and judges in London.
 
• It played a crucial role in shaping colonial law and ensuring uniformity in legal decisions across British territories.
 
 
 
• **Abolition of Privy Council Appeals**
 
 
• Post-independence, the appeals to the Privy Council were abolished through legislative measures.
 
• The Supreme Court of India became the highest judicial authority in the country.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court of India**
 
 
• Established on January 28, 1950, as the apex court of India under the Constitution.
 
• It replaced the Federal Court and took over the judicial functions previously held by the Privy Council.

questions.concept: Advent of Europeans
questions.question: Which of the following companies founded in 1602 is also known as the 'Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC)'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dutch East India Company**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Dutch East India Company, also known as **Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC)**, was established in the year **1602**.
 
• The VOC was the **first multinational corporation** in the world and the first company to issue stock publicly.
 
• It was created to **manage Dutch trade in the Indian Ocean region** and played a significant role in establishing Dutch colonial presence in Asia.
 
• The company held a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia, dealing primarily in spices, silk, tea, and other valuable commodities.
 
• The VOC's headquarters were located in **Amsterdam**, and it had a powerful fleet and military presence to protect its interests.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC):**

 
 
• The VOC is often considered as the precursor to modern corporations due to its innovative financial and organizational systems.
 
• It had the authority to **wage wars, negotiate treaties, mint coins, and establish colonies**.
 
• It was instrumental in the Dutch Golden Age, contributing significantly to the prosperity of the Netherlands during the 17th century.
 
 
 
• **Decline of the VOC:**
 
 
• The company began to decline in the 18th century due to corruption, mismanagement, and increased competition from other European nations.
 
• It was officially dissolved in **1799**, and its territories were taken over by the Dutch government.
 
 
 
• **Spice Trade:**
 
 
• The VOC was heavily involved in the lucrative spice trade, particularly nutmeg, cloves, and pepper, which were highly sought after in Europe.
 
• The company controlled several key ports and islands in Southeast Asia, such as the Moluccas and Batavia (modern-day Jakarta).
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• The VOC's model of joint-stock ownership and its global trade networks laid the foundation for modern capitalism and multinational corporations.
 
• Its influence shaped economic and political dynamics in Asia and Europe for centuries.

questions.concept: The Great Revolt of 1857
questions.question: Who among the following was the leader of the 1857 rebellion of Sambalpur?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Veer Surendra Sai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Veer Surendra Sai was a prominent freedom fighter and tribal leader from Sambalpur (present-day Odisha).
 
• He led the rebellion against British colonial rule in the Sambalpur region during the 1857 uprising, also known as the First War of Indian Independence.
 
• Surendra Sai fought to protect the rights of the tribal people and opposed British exploitation of resources and their oppressive policies.
 
• He was imprisoned multiple times by the British but continued to inspire resistance against colonial rule until his death in 1884.
 
• His leadership was instrumental in mobilizing the tribal communities of western Odisha for freedom, making him a revered figure in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sambalpur Rebellion:**

 
 
• The rebellion in Sambalpur was part of the larger 1857 revolt against British rule in India.
 
• It was marked by resistance from tribal leaders like Veer Surendra Sai, who fought for the restoration of local self-governance.
 
 
 
• **Veer Surendra Sai's Early Life:**
 
 
• He was born on January 23, 1809, in the Khinda village of Sambalpur.
 
• As a member of the Chauhan dynasty, he claimed the throne of Sambalpur after the death of Maharaja Sai in 1827.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Resistance:**
 
 
• Surendra Sai united several tribal communities, including the Binjhal, Gond, and Kol tribes, to oppose British authority.
 
• The tribal resistance was fueled by British attempts to impose taxes and exploit natural resources in the region.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Surendra Sai's resistance to British rule is celebrated in Odisha, and he is regarded as a hero of Indian independence.
 
• Several institutions, roads, and public spaces in Odisha are named after him to honor his contributions.
tags: The Great Revolt of 1857

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: The Mahalwari system was prevalent in certain regions of northern and central India. From whom was the land revenue collected under the Mahalwari system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Village head**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mahalwari system was introduced in 1833 by the British East India Company during the administration of **Lord William Bentinck**.
 
• Under this system, the **village headman (or Pradhan)** was made responsible for collecting land revenue from the farmers on behalf of the British government.
 
• The revenue settlement was made collectively for the village or estate, which was referred to as the "Mahal."
 
• This system was primarily implemented in parts of **North-Western Provinces, Central Provinces, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• The goal was to create a direct link between the colonial administration and the village community, while also ensuring the efficient collection of revenue.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Features of Mahalwari System:**

 
 
• The system combined elements of both the Zamindari and Ryotwari systems.
 
• Revenue rates were periodically revised, and the village collectively bore the responsibility of payment.
 
 
 
• **Zamindari System:**
 
 
• In this system, land revenue was collected by landlords (Zamindars) from the peasants and paid to the British government.
 
• It was introduced in Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha under the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793.
 
 
 
• **Ryotwari System:**
 
 
• Here, the settlement was directly made with the cultivators (Ryots), who were recognized as the owners of the land.
 
• It was primarily implemented in Madras, Bombay, and parts of Assam.
 
 
 
• **Purpose of Revenue Systems:**
 
 
• The primary objective of these systems was to extract maximum revenue for the British administration.
 
• However, these policies often led to exploitation and economic distress among Indian farmers.
tags: India under East India Company’s Rule

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: When was municipal governance first introduced in British India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1687**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Municipal governance was first introduced in British India in **1687**, with the establishment of the municipal corporation in **Madras (now Chennai).**
 
• The Madras Municipal Corporation was the **first attempt by the British to introduce local self-governance** in India.
 
• Following Madras, municipal governance was later extended to Bombay and Calcutta in the early 18th century.
 
• The introduction of municipal governance aimed to ensure better administration, sanitation, and infrastructure development in urban centers.
 
• It laid the foundation for modern urban governance in India, which later evolved through subsequent legislative reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Terminology:**

 
 
• **Municipal Corporation:** It is a form of urban local governance responsible for the administration of cities with large populations.
 
• **Local Self-Governance:** A system of governance where local authorities manage their own affairs independently within the framework of a larger governing system.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Municipal Governance:**
 
 
• In 1882, Lord Ripon introduced reforms to strengthen local self-governance, often referred to as the "Father of Local Self-Government in India."
 
• The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) further emphasized the importance of local governance under the provincial governments.
 
 
 
• **Modern Municipal Governance:**
 
 
• The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 provided a constitutional status to municipalities and introduced the concept of urban local bodies.
 
• It mandated the establishment of municipal corporations, municipal councils, and Nagar Panchayats based on population size.
 
 
 
• **Impact:**
 
 
• Municipal governance in India plays a key role in urban planning, infrastructure development, and the delivery of essential services.
 
• It ensures civic amenities such as water supply, waste management, street lighting, and public health services.

questions.concept: The Great Revolt of 1857
questions.question: The revolt of 1857 broke out on 10th May from which of the following places, when sepoys rose in rebellion and marched towards Delhi to restore Bahadur Shah II to the throne?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Meerut**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Revolt of 1857 began on **10th May 1857** in Meerut, located in present-day Uttar Pradesh, India.
 
• The immediate cause was the resentment among sepoys over the use of greased cartridges, which were rumored to be coated with cow and pig fat, offending both Hindu and Muslim religious sentiments.
 
• The sepoys of the East India Company stationed in Meerut refused to use the cartridges, leading to their court-martial, which ignited the rebellion.
 
• After revolting, the sepoys marched to Delhi and declared **Bahadur Shah II**, the last Mughal emperor, as their symbolic leader to unite Indians against British rule.
 
• The uprising in Meerut marked the beginning of the larger struggle, which spread to various parts of India such as Kanpur, Lucknow, and Jhansi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Causes of the Revolt:**

 
 
• **Political Causes:** Policies like the Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance alienated Indian rulers.
 
• **Economic Causes:** Exploitative land revenue systems and destruction of traditional industries hurt Indian peasants and artisans.
 
• **Social and Religious Causes:** Reforms like the abolition of Sati and the introduction of the Widow Remarriage Act created distrust among conservative Indians.
 
 
 
• **Key Leaders of the Revolt:**
 
 
• Rani Lakshmibai in Jhansi, Tantia Tope in Kanpur, and Begum Hazrat Mahal in Lucknow played significant roles in leading the rebellion.
 
 
 
• **Outcome of the Revolt:**
 
 
• The revolt was eventually suppressed by the British, and the East India Company was abolished in 1858.
 
• India came under the direct control of the British Crown, marking the beginning of the British Raj.
 
 
 
• **Historical Significance:**
 
 
• The Revolt of 1857 is often regarded as India's First War of Independence, despite its failure.
 
• It sowed the seeds for future resistance movements against British colonial rule.

questions.concept: The Great Revolt of 1857
questions.question: Which of the following key centres of the 1857 Revolt was recaptured from the rebel forces in September 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Delhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Delhi, a major center of the 1857 Revolt, was recaptured by British forces in **September 1857**.
 
• The siege of Delhi lasted from **June 8 to September 20, 1857**, and marked a critical turning point in the rebellion.
 
• The British forces, led by General John Nicholson, launched a decisive assault on the city, overcoming fierce resistance from the rebels.
 
• Delhi was significant as the symbolic seat of the Mughal Emperor, Bahadur Shah II, who was declared the nominal leader of the rebellion.
 
• The recapture of Delhi dealt a severe blow to the morale and coordination of the rebel forces during the uprising.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **1857 Revolt:** Also known as the First War of Indian Independence, it was a widespread rebellion against British rule.
 
• **Bahadur Shah II:** The last Mughal Emperor, who was declared the symbolic leader of the revolt, was later captured and exiled to Rangoon.
 
• **General John Nicholson:** A key British commander during the Siege of Delhi, he played a pivotal role in the city's recapture but was mortally wounded in the process.
 
• **Significance of Delhi:** As the center of Mughal power, Delhi held immense symbolic and strategic importance for both the rebels and the British.
 
• **Aftermath:** The recapture of Delhi marked the beginning of the suppression of the revolt, with other key centers like Kanpur, Lucknow, and Jhansi falling in the following months.

questions.concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
questions.question: What provision was sanctioned by the Charter Act of 1813?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Introduction of western sciences**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Charter Act of 1813 allowed for the **promotion of Western education** in India, including sciences and literature.
 
• This act sanctioned a sum of **₹1 lakh annually** for the education of Indians to encourage the introduction of Western knowledge.
 
• The Act ended the monopoly of the East India Company in trade, except for trade in tea and trade with China, which indirectly supported the spread of education and knowledge.
 
• It laid the foundation for **modern education** in India by emphasizing the need for institutions to teach Western sciences and languages.
 
• Missionaries were allowed under the Act to propagate Christianity, which also contributed to the spread of English education in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act of 1813**

 
 
• This Act was passed by the British Parliament to renew the charter of the East India Company.
 
• It marked a shift in British policy by introducing measures for the advancement of education in India.
 
• It also aimed to protect the rights of Indian subjects and bring changes in administrative governance.
 
 
 
• **Western Education in India**
 
 
• The Charter Act of 1813 was the first official step toward the establishment of English education in India.
 
• Western sciences and literature were introduced as part of a broader effort to modernize Indian education.
 
• It provided the groundwork for future educational reforms such as the Macaulay Minute of 1835.
 
 
 
• **Missionary Activities**
 
 
• The Act allowed Christian missionaries to enter India and propagate their religion.
 
• Missionaries were instrumental in establishing schools and colleges that taught Western sciences and languages.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Society**
 
 
• The introduction of Western sciences and literature helped Indians gain knowledge in various fields such as medicine, engineering, and law.
 
• It also contributed to the rise of a new educated middle class in India.
